identification.summary: Cyber Islamic Resistance (CIR) is a Telegram-based hacktivist persona described by Malpedia as ideologically aligned with Iran, engaged in website defacement, DDoS and data exfiltration claims against Israeli and Western entities, and as having claimed access to industrial control systems [S2]. Vendors describe it as an umbrella identity for smaller hacktivist groups that share resources and synchronize campaigns [S7], and CSIS argues more generally that Iran's hacktivist personas can mask state-coordinated activity [S3]. Reporting concentrates on the February-March 2026 Iran-Israel-US conflict [S4][S5][S8].
identification.notes: No source gathered gives a founding date; all retrieved reporting is from 2026. Name overlaps: Recorded Future's 2013 'Islamic Cyber Resistance' reporting concerns a different, earlier period and is not used as evidence here. A search summary also used 'Islamic Cyber Resistance' for the 313 Team; do not merge the two without primary evidence. Cyber Jihad Movement (al-Qaeda-affiliated) is a separate actor [S5].

attribution.confidence: No government attribution located. CSIS argues generally that Iranian hacktivist personas can front state operations and that hacktivist TTPs increasingly resemble state APTs [S3]; the search summary seen did not confirm that CSIS names CIR specifically. This is an analyst assessment, not an official finding.
attribution.basis: Self-presentation as Iran-aligned [S2]; analyst assessments of coordination [S3][S7][S10]. A joint claim signed by CIR, 313 Team, FAD Team, Cyber Fatteh Team and others was reported in March 2026 [S9]. No technical forensics tying CIR to IRGC or MOIS were found.

objectives: Disruption, psychological and reputational impact against Israeli and Western targets, framed as retaliation and 'mobilization' during the 2026 conflict [S2][S8]. Rapid7 treats such visible activity as possible signaling, pressure and preparatory shaping rather than isolated nuisance [S1].

sectors: Israeli defense industry (Rafael air-defense and drone-detection claims) [S6]
Civil alerting (Home Front Command app claim) [S8]
regions: Gulf states, including a Qatari company website in a joint claim [S4][S9]
targeting.notes: Target lists come from the group's own claims relayed by trackers and press; most are unverified [S2][S4][S6].

capabilities.summary: Primary activity is DDoS, defacement, claimed intrusion and information operations [S2][S4]. Rapid7 characterizes the wider Iran-linked ecosystem as relying on established techniques (phishing, credential access, DDoS, edge-device compromise) rather than novel exploits [S1]. CIR reportedly participated in an Electronic Operations Room, a Telegram coordination hub set up 2026-02-28 that coordinated more than 50 hacktivist cells [S4]. OT/ICS access claims (PLC controllers, energy dashboards, 2026-03-02) were treated as unverified by analysts [S4].

campaigns.name: Electronic Operations Room formation
campaigns.summary: Cyble reports a Telegram umbrella coordinating more than 50 hacktivist cells was established as US and Israeli strikes began; CIR is reported as part of it.

campaigns.name: Claimed attacks on Rafael systems and ICS/OT access
campaigns.summary: Euronews reports a group it calls the 'Islamic Cyber Resistance Axis' (reported here as CIR) claimed attacks on Israeli defense firm Rafael's air defense systems and the VigilAir drone-detection service; Cyble reports claims of access to PLC controllers and energy dashboards, treated as unverified.

campaigns.name: Home Front Command app 'general mobilization' claim
campaigns.summary: FalconFeeds reports the CIR Telegram channel announced a 'general mobilization' and cited reports of a malfunction in Israel's Home Front Command alert app; link between the malfunction and CIR is unverified.

campaigns.name: Joint claim against Qatari company website
campaigns.summary: A claim signed by CIR, 313 Team, FAD Team, Cyber Fatteh Team and others was reported; one Kurdish member later withdrew from the coalition.

campaigns.name: Claimed breach of Israeli cybersecurity firm
campaigns.summary: CIR is reported to have published batches of allegedly exfiltrated files and database exports; claim unverified.

diamond.adversary: Self-described Iran-aligned hacktivist persona; sponsor unproven, with analyst assessments of coordination [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: DDoS with downtime proofs, defacement, claimed data theft, claimed ICS/OT access, information operations [S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channels and coalition hubs (Electronic Operations Room) for command, claims and propaganda [S4][S8]; DDoS-for-hire style tooling reported but not verified.
diamond.victim: Israeli security firms, defense industry, academia and civil alerting; Gulf government and commercial sites [S2][S4][S6][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Wartime retaliation narrative during the 2026 Iran-Israel-US conflict; coalition messaging amplifies psychological effect [S1][S8].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web services, exposed OT/ICS and mobile alerting apps are the claimed exposure points [S4][S8].

gaps: No WebFetch access was available (host resolution failed), so all sources were read through search-result summaries only; Rapid7, SOCRadar, Malpedia, CSIS, Outpost24, Sophos and FalconFeeds pages were not opened in full.
No founding date, leadership, or state sponsor is established; the IRGC/MOIS link is analyst inference for the ecosystem, not for CIR specifically [S3].
ICS/OT, breach and Home Front Command app claims are unverified self-claims; no victim confirmation or technical indicators found.
Boundaries with 313 Team, FAD Team, Cyber Fattah and the Electronic Operations Room are blurred; an 'Islamic Cyber Resistance' label is also used elsewhere.
Exact publication dates for the CSIS, LevelBlue and Outpost24 items were not seen.
Activity after the April 2026 provisional ceasefire is not documented in gathered sources [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing web portals, civil alerting apps and exposed OT/ICS devices in Israel and the Gulf, plus the Telegram channels used for coordination [S4][S8]. STEP 2: The actor operates as a loose coalition persona whose claims outrun verified effect; its signal is mostly psychological [S1][S7]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is DDoS and defacement with downtime proof, breach-claim leaks, and OT access claims posted on Telegram [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-impact DDoS, defacement and exaggerated claims timed to kinetic events. MDCOA is that a real state-directed access to OT is fronted by the persona, as CSIS notes for other Iranian personas [S3]. Candidate indicators: Telegram mobilization posts, coalition-signed joint claims, check-host downtime proofs, and spikes in DDoS against Gulf government sites [S4][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor Telegram claims but triage them as unverified until victims or telemetry confirm [S4]. (2) Authorities: persona activity may be state-directed, so coordinate with intelligence and law enforcement partners before response decisions [S3]. (3) Mission assurance: verify exposure of internet-facing OT and web services at supported installations and partner nations, and plan DDoS mitigation [S4]. (4) Coordination: share claims with regional partners and the information-operations community to counter inflated narratives [S8].
